notes:
I've got notes on every verse except 7 and 9, which only got brief mentions. Several sources were cut off partway: Gill stops around v. 19, Guzik's main page around v. 14, and I only saw the opening of the Precept Austin page (though search snippets added some later material). I ran out of searches before I could check wesley.nnu.edu, oca.org, newadvent.org, bibleodyssey.org, the Lutheran sites, or the Pentecostal sites other than Enduring Word. Those gaps are listed at the end.

**v. 1**
- Guzik says the Kadesh here may be a different place from the Kadesh of Numbers 13:26. Either way, the name recalls Israel's earlier failure of faith there. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-20/
- He reads Miriam's death as God keeping His word that the generation that refused to enter Canaan would die in the wilderness. Moses' own family got no exception. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-20/
- Date: the year isn't given. The NET note and the UBS Handbook both think it is probably the fortieth year, the last of the journey. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-20-commentary
- Gill notes that, unlike Aaron and Moses, no mourning for Miriam is recorded. He suggests the people were too distressed about the lack of water. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-20.html
- Clarke (Methodist) mentions that Catholic writers made Miriam a type of the Virgin Mary. He also says the three siblings all died within about a year. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/numbers/20.htm

**v. 2**
- Gill says God withheld water to test whether this new generation would behave better than their parents had in Exodus 17. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-20.html
- Jamieson points out that Kadesh had a spring, so the lack of water was unusual. https://biblehub.com/library/jamieson/commentary_critical_and_explanatory_on_the_whole_bible/nu_20_1-29_the_death_of.htm
- Guzik calls it a real need, but says the people turned against their leaders instead of trusting God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-20/

**v. 3**
- The NET note says the Hebrew verb for "quarreled" can mean a formal legal complaint. It calls this something deliberate and argued, far worse than grumbling. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Num&chapter=20
- Gill takes "our brothers" to mean those who died at Taberah or with Korah. He says the people were brothers in sin as well as in blood. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-20.html
- Guzik says the younger generation was starting to act like the unbelieving older one. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-20/

**v. 4**
- Gill says the people echo their parents' words, which shows how strongly a bad example passes down to children. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-20.html
- Guzik says they went so far as to accuse Moses and Aaron of planning their deaths. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-20/

**v. 5**
- Guzik says they could only see what the wilderness lacked compared with Canaan, not God's provision there. Ironically, they would never reach that abundance unless they learned to trust God in the wilderness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-20/
- Gill says they talk as if Moses forced them out of Egypt, forgetting their slavery. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-20.html

**v. 6**
- Gill, following the medieval Jewish scholar Aben Ezra, thinks Moses and Aaron withdrew partly out of fear of being stoned, and fell down to pray for the people's forgiveness. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-20.html
- Guzik says they saw the danger that the new generation could end up as faithless as the old. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-20/

**v. 8**
- Guzik's key point: God told Moses to take the staff but not to use it, only to speak. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-20/
- Gill says this was Moses' own staff of miracles, not Aaron's budding rod. He thinks this was a different rock from the one at Horeb, and that the command tested the faith of Moses and Aaron. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-20.html

**v. 10**
- Guzik says God never told Moses to lecture the people. On earlier occasions Moses had fallen on his face or cried out to God instead. He also notes that "we" seems to make Moses and Aaron the ones giving the water. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-20/
- Gill reads "must we…" as doubt, not about God's power but about whether God was willing to help such rebels, spoken in anger (Psalm 106:32). https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-20.html
- Precept Austin adds that Moses was worn out and grieving Miriam, and was taking glory that belonged to God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62372/

**v. 11**
- Guzik: Moses disobeyed outright, and in anger struck twice where the earlier rock was struck only once. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-20/
- He adds that God still gave water in abundance, so being used by God doesn't prove God is pleased. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-20/
- Gill and Guzik both report the Jewish Targum legend that the first blow drew blood. Gill links it, tentatively, to the blood and water from Christ's side. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-20.html

**v. 12: the main point of disagreement**
- **Standard evangelical view (GotQuestions):** Moses disobeyed a direct command, took credit for the miracle, and did it in public. https://www.gotquestions.org/Moses-promised-land.html
- **Typology (seeing the rock as a picture of Christ):**
  - GotQuestions: the rock pictures Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4). He was struck once, so speaking was the fitting picture of prayer, and striking again in effect crucified Him again. https://www.gotquestions.org/Moses-promised-land.html
  - Guzik (Calvary Chapel, the Pentecostal/charismatic-leaning site on your list) makes the same argument. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-20/
- **Unbelief as the root sin:**
  - Bible.org: unbelief was the root, and Moses' long-standing anger problem fed it. It also cites Charles Simeon (Anglican): Moses stands for the Law, and one breach of the Law is enough to condemn. https://bible.org/seriespage/26-stumbling-finish-numbers-201-13
  - Guzik lists the faults involved: rash grief, taking credit, showing God as angry when He wasn't, among others. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-20/
- **Gill (Baptist) disagrees with "striking was the sin."** God told Moses to take the rod, and striking would only make Moses guilty, not Aaron. Gill also rejects calling the people "rebels" as the sin, since God had used that word Himself. He concludes the sin was unbelief: doubting that God was willing to help such a people. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-20.html
- **Coke (Methodist)** names two sins: unbelief, and impatience shown in calling the people rebels and striking hard. Seeing the rod used only as a sign elsewhere, he notes some think striking at all, not just twice, showed distrust. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tcc/numbers-20.html
- **Pulpit Commentary** (largely Anglican writers) says Moses can't have doubted God's power. Striking twice was a sign of anger and would hardly matter on its own. What counted was the bad impression it made on the people. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/numbers-20.html
- **Constable (Dallas Seminary)** records the view that Moses' words, not the striking, were the real wrong. He doesn't think the text supports it, and says the seriousness came from Moses' office. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-20.html
- **Catholic:**
  - Catholic.com: Moses and Aaron fell back on a method that had worked before. That showed a lack of faith and arguably superstition (it cites the Catechism, para. 2111). https://www.catholic.com/qa/in-numbers-20-why-did-moses-and-aaron-sin-when-they-struck-the-rock
  - Haydock's commentary (citing Challoner) says the fault was a weakness of faith, not doubt of God's power. It says Augustine did not think them guilty of grievous sin, and reads the two blows as the two beams of the cross. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-20.html
- **The punishment was temporal:** BibleHub's Q&A says Moses still appears at the Transfiguration. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_couldn_t_Moses_enter_Promised_Land.htm

**v. 13**
- Guzik: Moses failed to honour God as holy, but God showed Himself holy by correcting him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-20/
- Gill: this is called Meribah-Kadesh to tell it apart from the Horeb Meribah. The Targum and the medieval Jewish scholar Rashi read "showed His holiness" as God not sparing His own saints. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-20.html
- Haydock: God showed mercy to the people and fair severity to His ministers. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-20.html

**vv. 14–16**
- Guzik says this begins the last stage of the Exodus, bringing Israel closer to Canaan than ever before. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-20/
- Gill: "your brother Israel" appeals to the kinship of Jacob and Esau, and the hardships are told to win Edom's sympathy. He takes the "angel" to be the Angel of God's presence from the burning bush, not Moses, as some Jewish writers held. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-20.html

**v. 17**
- Gill: Israel promises to stay out of private fields and wells. He reads the King's Highway as the public road. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-20.html
- The NET note describes it as the main road from Damascus to the Gulf of Aqaba. Bronze Age forts found along it show it existed in Moses' time. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Num&chapter=20

**vv. 18–19**
- Gill: Edom threatens an armed force. Israel offers to pay for water, which he says was normal where water was scarce. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-20.html

**vv. 20–21**
- BibleHub's topical article: Edom's refusal forced Israel onto a longer route around Edom. https://biblehub.com/topical/t/the_king's_highway.htm

**vv. 22–23**
- Gill: "Mount Hor" literally means "the mountain of the mountain." God spoke while the people were camped at its foot. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-20.html
- The NET note gives other proposed locations, including Jebel Madurah near Kadesh. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Num&chapter=20

**v. 24**
- Guzik: Aaron was given time to prepare for his death. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-20/
- Jamieson: the punishment brought Aaron's death sooner, but its manner was arranged tenderly and to honour him. https://biblehub.com/library/jamieson/commentary_critical_and_explanatory_on_the_whole_bible/nu_20_1-29_the_death_of.htm

**vv. 25–26**
- Calvin (Reformed): a public handover settled who was the lawful priest, so this changeable people could not pick a priest from another tribe. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/20-25.html
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: the robes were removed so they would not be defiled by contact with the dead. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/20-25.html
- Clarke: removing the robes took away Aaron's office and gave it to Eleazar. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/numbers-20.html

**vv. 27–28**
- Gill: the same hands that first robed Aaron now unrobe him. This also points ahead to Aaron's priesthood being set aside when the Messiah came. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/20-28.htm
- Matthew Henry: death strips us all. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/20-28.html
- Guzik: the man died but the priesthood went on, which he says points to Jesus as the everlasting high priest. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-20/
- Ellicott on the BibleHub page: Aaron's death showed the Levitical priesthood was imperfect. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/20-28.htm
- Deuteronomy 10:6 says Aaron died at Moserah. Gleason Archer raises the problem. Benson and Poole solve it by treating Moserah as the wider area and Mount Hor as a spot within it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-20-commentary and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/20-28.htm

**v. 29**
- Gill: the people knew Aaron was dead from what Moses told them and from seeing Eleazar wearing the robes. They did not see the body. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-20.html
- Pett: thirty days seems to have been the usual mourning for a great leader. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/pet/numbers-20.html
- Guzik: Moses (the Law), Miriam (the prophets) and Aaron (the priesthood) could not bring Israel in. Only Joshua, whose name is the Hebrew form of "Jesus," could. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-20/

**What I couldn't find**
- **Wesley, Lutheran and Orthodox sources:** none checked (wesley.nnu.edu, lcms.org, 1517.org, oca.org). The Methodist view above comes from Clarke and Coke instead.
- **Modern scholarship:** nothing from bibleodyssey.org.
- **Popular modern teaching:** nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings.
